results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve). The optic nerve can be shown by MRI, OCT or VEP. The kappa free light chain index is accepted alongside CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. The central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions are supporting MRI markers.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

results.authors: Wattjes MP, Ciccarelli O, Reich DS, et al.
results.key_findings: Diagnostic MRI should include the brain with 3D FLAIR, T2 and pre- and post-gadolinium T1, and the spinal cord with at least two sagittal sequences, ideally in the same session.
results.title: 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in patients with multiple sclerosis

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended. AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG should be tested by cell-based assay when NMOSD or MOGAD is a consideration.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
Do not dismiss the earlier right arm and trunk sensory episode as cervical radiculopathy: it is a prior attack with residual sensory signs and a matching C3-C4 dorsal-column lesion
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord and left optic nerve: five regions, so no separate DIT is required).

Offer high-dose methylprednisolone for the disabling left optic neuritis (acuity 20/80): oral 500 mg daily for 5 days or, as an inpatient, IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days; advise her to stop as-needed ibuprofen during the course (gastrointestinal bleeding risk); consider plasma exchange if severe visual loss does not respond.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 6 months, enhancing optic nerve, periventricular and T6-T7 cord lesions, lesions in 5 of 5 regions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check full blood count with lymphocyte count, liver function, HBsAg and anti-HBc, hepatitis C and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before treatment starts
Supplement vitamin D for the low 25-OH level (21 ng/mL) as general health advice, and explain the heat-related transient worsening she already reports (Uhthoff phenomenon).

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure or altered awareness; EEG does not contribute to the evaluation of optic neuritis or cord lesions.
CT does not show demyelinating lesions; she needs MRI of the brain, orbits and cord, not CT.
No cardiac symptom or finding; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
No palpitations or syncope; rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
FDG-PET does not distinguish demyelination from its mimics and adds nothing to MS-protocol MRI.

differential.key_features: AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay; unilateral optic neuritis with acuity 20/80; cord lesions shorter than one segment and peripheral; six CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands
MOG-IgG negative by live cell-based assay; unilateral optic neuritis with a 12 mm intraorbital segment and no perineural enhancement; no ADEM-like or conus lesions; oligoclonal bands present
No leptomeningeal enhancement, normal calcium, no systemic features; ovoid periventricular and juxtacortical lesions are typical of MS rather than granulomatous disease
B12 444 pg/mL and MCV 89.8 fL; focal enhancing cord and brain lesions are not explained by B12 deficiency
ANA negative; no rash, arthritis, oral ulcers or other systemic features
No encephalopathy; two attacks six months apart; discrete ovoid lesions rather than large confluent ones
No encephalopathy, hearing loss or branch retinal artery occlusion; no central callosal lesions

key_clinical_evidence: Acute painful left optic neuritis (acuity 20/80, left RAPD, red desaturation, normal disc) with an enhancing, mildly swollen 12 mm intraorbital segment of the left optic nerve on MRI and a prolonged left P100 (128 ms).

DIS: 5 of 5 regions: periventricular (bilateral ovoid lesions, enhancing lesion at the right lateral ventricle body), juxtacortical (right frontal, left parietal), infratentorial (left middle cerebellar peduncle), spinal cord (C3-C4 dorsal columns, T6-T7 left lateral column), optic nerve (left). With five regions no separate DIT or CSF is needed; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexist on the same scans.
Prior attack 6 months ago: 3 weeks of right arm and band-like trunk numbness, with residual right arm and T4-T8 sensory loss and Lhermitte sign, matching the C3-C4 dorsal-column lesion.
Left hip flexor weakness, left extensor plantar and left heel-to-shin ataxia match the left lateral-column T6-T7 lesion and the left middle cerebellar peduncle lesion.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, short peripheral cord lesions and six CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (kFLC index 38.5) argue against NMOSD and MOGAD.
Low 25-OH vitamin D (21 ng/mL) is a risk factor and comorbidity; it does not explain the lesions.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sarah Lindgren is a 28-year-old right-handed woman who presents with a 3-day history of progressive vision loss in her left eye accompanied by retro-orbital pain that worsens with eye movement. She first noticed blurred vision in her left eye while reading on her tablet three evenings ago and initially attributed it to fatigue after a long day at work. Over the following 24 hours the vision in her left eye continued to deteriorate, and she noticed that colors, particularly reds and oranges, appeared washed out when viewed through the left eye compared to the right. She also developed a dull aching pain behind her left eye that is exacerbated by lateral and upward gaze. By the morning of presentation, she could no longer read print with the left eye and became alarmed, prompting her partner to bring her to the emergency department. On further questioning, she reports that approximately six months ago she experienced a three-week episode of numbness and tingling involving her right arm and the right side of her trunk, which she describes as a band-like sensation around her ribcage. She saw her primary care physician at that time who suspected a pinched nerve and recommended over-the-counter analgesics. The numbness gradually improved but she notes that she still has intermittent tingling in the right hand, particularly when she is tired or overheated. She also reports that over the past several months she has experienced unusual fatigue that is disproportionate to her activity level, and she has occasionally noticed that her left leg feels heavy after prolonged walking or exercise, though she has not fallen. She denies fevers, weight loss, rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, or other systemic symptoms. She denies any prior episodes of vision loss, diplopia, dysphagia, or bowel and bladder dysfunction.
